newsitem.title: FINLAND: Merita CEO says profits can improve - RFTV.
newsitem.headline: Merita CEO says profits can improve - RFTV.

text.p: Finnish banking group Merita Oy chief executive Vesa Vainio said on Thursday he saw good possibilities for improving profitability and that a potential share buy-back scheme had to wait until this came about.

"We have no actual plans for such an operation now. I guess we have to improve our profits first," Vainio told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV) in an interview. He was responding to a question about a possible share buy-back.
"We see good possibilities for improving profitability of the bank," Vainio said.
Merita earlier reported a 93 percent jump in January-September group operating profit after credit losses to 930 million markka.
The banking group, Finland's biggest, said it expected to be able to pay a dividend on its full-year 1996 result -- the first pay-out to shareholders in five years.
Asked whether credit demand would grow in 1997, Vainio said:
"Somewhat, yes. We are not in for any very rapid increase in credit demand, but still some demand."
In the first nine months, Merita's net income from financial operations rose 9.8 percent on the year-ago period to 3.03 billion markka.

Merita Bank's income-to-costs ratio rose to 1.46 in January-September from 1.37 in 1995. Vainio said the ratio would improve further because "we will see the cost-saving impact of our merger fully first at the end of next year."
The group's burden of non-performing receivables had "developed quite well," Vainio said, pointing to the end-September figure of 5.03 billion markka, down from 7.34 billion at end-1995.
In the interim report, Merita said the "trend in loan losses has been more favourable than expected".
The Finnish real estate market did not look like picking up soon, but Vainio nevertheless saw opportunities.

"The real estate market is difficult in all European countries. On the other hand, (the) rental market is improving in Finland now so we see some possibilities to improve our profits and our rental income especially," he said.
Vainio said he was "comfortable and confident" with Merita's capital adequacy ratio -- 10.8 percent at end-September, up from 10.3 percent at the end of 1995.

The third phase of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union, due to begin in 1999, would cause adjustment costs and dent income, especially in foreign exchange trading, the bank said, but Vainio also saw new revenue growth opportunities for Merita.

"On the balance, we are waiting for new possibilities on some new products and, of course, the capital markets will be much deeper for Finns and Finnish banks also in the future so I guess we can get some new revenues also," he told RFTV.
